description.summary: A multi-headed serpentine monster from Greek mythology. Famous as the Lernaean Hydra defeated by Hercules in his second labor. Known for regenerating two heads when one is cut off.
description.full: The Hydra is a legendary multi-headed serpent from Greek mythology, most famously known as the Lernaean Hydra that Hercules faced as his second labor. Typically depicted with nine heads, the Hydra possessed the terrifying ability to regenerate two new heads whenever one was severed. Its breath and blood were poisonous, and one of its heads was immortal. Hercules defeated it by cauterizing the neck stumps after beheading to prevent regeneration, and burying the immortal head under a boulder. The Hydra has become a powerful symbol for problems that multiply when confronted, representing exponential difficulty and insurmountable challenges.

etymology.origin: From Greek 'hydra' (ὕδρα), meaning 'water serpent', from 'hydor' (ὕδωρ) meaning 'water'.

history.modern_era: The Hydra remains one of the most recognizable Greek monsters. The term 'hydra' is used metaphorically for any problem that becomes worse when addressed. It appears in modern media, comics (Marvel's HYDRA organization), and is widely used in scientific naming.

famous_myth.title: The Second Labor of Hercules
famous_myth.summary: Hercules was tasked with slaying the Lernaean Hydra as his second labor. Each time he cut off one of its heads, two more grew back. With the help of his nephew Iolaus, Hercules cauterized each neck stump with a firebrand after decapitation, preventing regeneration. The immortal head he buried under a heavy boulder. Hercules then dipped his arrows in the Hydra's poisonous blood, making them forever deadly.
famous_myth.outcome: Victory for Hercules, though Eurystheus did not count the labor as valid since Hercules had help from Iolaus
famous_myth.legacy: The poisoned arrows from Hydra's blood were used in subsequent labors and eventually caused Hercules' own death
